title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, and Evidence Workflows
author: Maya Thompson
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s standards and operational procedures for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure SDLC requirements, security-focused incident response procedures, compliance evidence collection workflows, and risk / exception handling. The guidance below is intended for engineering, platform, product security reviewers, and compliance owners.

Goals and scope
- Ensure least-privilege access and auditable authentication for humans and service principals.
- Provide end-to-end audit logging with integrity guarantees and demonstrable retention policies for compliance reviews.
- Define controls for customer data residency and retention aligned with contractual obligations.
- Embed security gates into the SDLC to prevent regressions and maintain evidence for audits.
- Provide a clear, repeatable incident response path that preserves evidentiary artifacts and supports post-incident compliance reporting.
- Define a risk exceptions process with owner, timeline, and compensating controls.

1) RBAC & Authentication (Summary)

Principles
- Principle of least privilege: grant the minimum permissions required for the task.
- Role-based alignment: prefer roles and groups over individual grants.
- Just-in-Time (JIT) elevation for high-privilege actions.
- Strong authentication: SSO (SAML/OIDC) + enforced MFA for all human users.
- Machine identities: short-lived tokens for services, centrally managed by Vault/KMS.

Roles and permissions (canonical list)
- reader: view-only access to dashboards, docs, and non-sensitive metadata.
- developer: deploy non-production jobs, read access to non-sensitive runtime metadata.
- operator: deploy to production, monitor, and remediate incidents for assigned services.
- admin: tenant-level management (team admin, billing, IAM).
- auditor: read-only access to audit logs, configuration manifests, and compliance evidence.

Authentication & provisioning
- Primary SSO provider: Okta (SAML 2.0 / OIDC).
- SCIM provisioning to automatically map directory groups to Redwood roles.
- MFA requirement: TOTP or hardware token (recommended YubiKey) enforced by Okta policy.
- Service accounts: created via central service-account API; tokens are ephemeral (default TTL 1h) and refresh via Vault (HashiCorp Vault integration).
- Privileged access: JIT sessions requested in the access portal (approval workflow via PagerDuty/SLA-based approver lists), session duration default 1 hour; extensions must be justified and logged.

RBAC policy example (policy-as-code snippet)
- Example (Terraform/HCL style; illustrative only):

  resource "redwood_iam_role" "operator" {
    name = "operator"
    permissions = ["service.deploy", "service.read", "incident.respond"]
    assigned_groups = ["okta:team-platform"]
  }

Ownership and reviews
- IAM owner: security/iam@redwood.com
- Quarterly access reviews required for all admin, operator, and auditor roles.
- Onboarding/Offboarding: HR hook + SCIM deprovisioning within 1 hour of termination ticket.

2) Audit Logging

Scope and requirements
- Capture: authentication events, role/permission changes, API calls that mutate state (create/update/delete), infra deployments, model-onboarding changes, and data export events.
- Integrity: logs are written to an append-only store with MD5/SHA256 checksums and periodic notarization.
- Availability SLO: audit ingestion success >= 99.99% over a 30d rolling window.
- Ingestion latency: 95th percentile <= 5s from event emit to persistent store.

Storage and retention
- Primary storage: secure cluster (internal name: audit-cluster-prod) feeding into long-term archive (S3: s3://redwood-audit-archive).
- Retention default: 365 days for operational logs; extended retention available for legal/customer contracts (e.g., 7 years).
- Tamper-evidence: daily signed digests stored in KMS-backed bucket.

Access and auditing
- Access to audit logs restricted to auditor, ops, and security roles.
- Access operations are themselves logged and require justification; viewing raw audit logs requires approval recorded in the access portal.

Example log schema (JSON line example)
{
  "timestamp": "2027-10-12T15:23:04Z",
  "service": "inference-router",
  "actor": "user:alice@example.com",
  "action": "model.deploy",
  "resource": "model:v2.1.3",
  "request_id": "req-3a4b5c6d"
}

Log integrity verification (daily)
1. Generate SHA256 digest for each day’s log bundle.
2. Sign digest with KMS key: projects/redwood/keys/audit-signing.
3. Publish signed digest to s3://redwood-audit-archive/digests/ and record in the compliance ledger.

3) Data Residency & Retention

Principles
- Customer data residency commitments are honored at tenant and dataset levels.
- Default residency: US (us-west-2); EU customers may opt into EU-only regions (eu-west-1 / europe-central).
- Cross-region replication is disabled for restricted tenants unless explicitly contractually allowed.

Controls
- Enforcement: deployment layer (router + tenancy service) enforces region-scoped routing. Any cross-region replication request requires a signed SLA amendment.
- Data classification: sensitive, regulated, and general. Regulations map to retention and isolation controls.

Retention policy table
| Data type | Default retention | Extended retention | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Audit logs | 365 days | Contract-specific (e.g., 7y) | Tamper-evident archive |
| Customer payloads (inference inputs) | 30 days | Customer-configurable; opt-in for longer retention | Default is ephemeral unless customer opts-in |
| Model artifacts (customer-owned) | 1 year | Customer-managed backups recommended | Snapshot schedule annotated in onboarding |
| Backups (infra config) | 90 days | 1 year for legal hold | Encrypted at rest |

Data deletion and legal holds
- Standard deletion flow: automated retention job deletes or overwrites data per policy. Deletions are logged and retention jobs produce signed proof artifacts.
- Legal hold: when a legal hold is issued, retention job marks tenant artifacts as "hold" and moves data to protected bucket with extended retention. Legal holds are timeboxed and owned by Legal with a named contact.

4) Secure SDLC (Security Gates & Evals)

Embedding security in SDLC
- Mandatory security reviews for: public API changes, infra changes affecting multi-tenancy, model onboarding, and storage changes.
- Pull request checks (CI) include: static analysis (SAST), dependency scanning (Snyk/OSS-Fuzz), container image vulnerability scan, and infrastructure plan validation.
- Required approvals: code owners + security reviewer for sensitive PRs.

Pre-deploy checks
1. CI gates: unit tests, integration tests, SAST, dependency scan (fail on CVSS >= 7.0 for new dependencies).
2. Canary rollout plan exists for any production-facing change > 0.5% traffic impact.
3. Automated fuzzing and load tests for runtime changes that touch the inference path.

Security checklist (example)
- Threat model updated for changes that introduce new network paths.
- Secrets are not present in code or images (check with repo scanners).
- Required encryption-at-rest settings validated in infra plan.
- SLO impact assessed and rollback playbook prepared.

5) Incident Response: Security Procedures

Triage and initial response
- Signal sources: monitoring alerts (Prometheus/Alertmanager), SLO breaches, PagerDuty, customer reports, or security tools (WAF, IDS).
- Initial severity assessment: use security severity matrix (Appendix A).
- Notify incident commander (IC) via PagerDuty and create incident in the IR platform (Atlassian Ops or internal tracker).

Containment and evidence preservation
- Containment steps must prioritize preservation of evidence: snapshot relevant hosts, preserve audit logs, freeze write access to affected S3 prefixes, and take forensic images as needed.
- For suspected data exfiltration: enable enhanced logging (VPC flow logs, API gateway logs), create immutable copies of the suspect data, and preserve network captures for up to 30 days.

Communication and compliance reporting
- Security will coordinate legal and communications for any event meeting breach criteria.
- Regulatory reporting windows (example): GDPR personal data breach notification within 72 hours following confirmation.
- Customer notification: follow contract and security incident SLA templates; coordinate via Customer Success and Legal.

Post-incident activities
- Postmortem: within 7 business days, IR lead to publish a draft postmortem with timeline, root cause analysis, and corrective actions.
- Evidence retention: artifacts preserved per legal hold / retention rules until closure.
- Lessons learned: implement remediation as tracked Jira tickets with owners and verification tests.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Required artifacts for audits
- IAM snapshots (roles, policies) as of the audit date.
- Audit log digests and signed copies for the audit period.
- Change history for infra (Terraform state) and model onboarding manifests.
- SDLC evidence: CI job runs, SCA/SAST results, and approval records for relevant PRs.
- Incident artifacts when applicable: incident ticket, timeline, containment steps, and customer communications.

Evidence collection process
1. Request initiation: compliance owner opens evidence request in the compliance portal.
2. Automated gatherers: scripts (compliance-collector) gather Terraform state, IAM exports, and signed log bundles.
3. Manual artifacts: owners attach design docs, threat models, and security review notes.
4. Evidence review: security + legal review and mark items as validated.
5. Delivery: produce a signed packet (ZIP) with manifest and hashes; upload to secure evidence bucket and record delivery in the compliance ledger.

7) Risk Exceptions and Compensating Controls

Process
- Exception request: via the risk exceptions form (link in portal) with owner, rationale, duration, and proposed compensating controls.
- Review cadence: Security board reviews exceptions weekly; high-risk exceptions require CISO approval.
- Expiry and re-evaluation: exceptions are timeboxed (max 90 days) and require renewal with new justification.

Typical compensating controls
- Network isolation tunnel for service-to-service access instead of role elevation.
- Enhanced monitoring and alerting on the affected resource.
- Temporary JIT-only access windows with logged approvals.

Tracking and auditability
- All exceptions are recorded in the risk register with a unique identifier (RISK-YYYY-XXXX) and include evidence of compensating controls.

8) Ownership, SLAs and Contacts

Owners
- Security lead (policy & IAM): security/iam@redwood.com
- Audit logging owner: infra-logging@redwood.com
- Data residency & retention: legal-compliance@redwood.com
- SDLC gates owner: eng-devex@redwood.com
- Incident Response lead: sec-incident@redwood.com

Operational SLAs
- Audit ingestion SLO: 99.99% success over 30d.
- Audit query latency: 95th percentile <= 2s for metadata queries.
- Evidence request turnaround: 5 business days for standard requests; 48 hours for high-priority audit requests.

Appendix A: Security severity matrix (summary)
- Sev 1 (Critical): confirmed data exfiltration of customer PII or active remote code execution in production.
- Sev 2 (High): suspected compromise affecting production data integrity or availability with significant customer impact.
- Sev 3 (Medium): security issues limited to non-production or isolated systems.
- Sev 4 (Low): minor vulnerabilities or informational findings.

Appendix B: CLI examples
- Export IAM roles (example):
  redwood iam export --output iam-snapshot-$(date +%F).json --roles admin,operator,auditor

- Trigger evidence collector (example):
  ./scripts/compliance-collector --start 2027-09-01 --end 2027-09-30 --output evidence-packet-sept2027.zip
